analysis.one_liner: Closes Atlantic and Gulf waters to longline fishing and buys out permits to rebuild overfished swordfish and marlin.
analysis.headline: Backed by one Republican sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to a House fisheries subcommittee in June 2000 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban a fishing method called pelagic longlining — long lines strung with hundreds of hooks — from large parts of the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico during key seasons. Government scientists had found swordfish, marlin, sailfish, and large coastal sharks were overfished, and longlines catch many of these fish (and young swordfish) accidentally. Fishermen who depended on the closed areas could accept a government payment — $50,000 plus up to $400,000 based on their best year's catch — in exchange for surrendering their permits forever. The buyout would be paid with $30 million in federal money plus a $20 million loan, repaid through fees on swordfish dealers and small fees or permit payments on recreational fishing.
analysis.who_benefits: Recreational anglers who fish for marlin and swordfish, since longlines kill large numbers of these fish as accidental catch; the commercial hand-gear swordfish fleet, which would receive the quota taken away from bought-out longline boats; and the public, which owns the fish, through rebuilt fish populations. The bill's own findings say the closures would also reduce conflict between commercial and recreational fishermen.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Recreational anglers and coastal fish stocks

how_it_helps.text: The bill cites government and international assessments that North Atlantic swordfish was at 65% of the biomass needed for a sustainable fishery, blue marlin at 24%, and white marlin at 23%, and would close longlining in those grounds to cut the death toll of young swordfish and marlin [S3].

Fishermen who had depended on the closed areas could sell their permits for $50,000 plus a payment of up to $400,000 based on their best landing year from 1992–1998, so the conservation burden would not fall on their families alone [S3].
The swordfish quota freed up by bought-out longline boats would be handed to the smaller commercial hand-gear fleet, which catches fish one at a time with far less accidental kill [S3].
The bill would also fund research into fishing gear that catches fewer marlin, sharks, and sea turtles by accident, with federal observers placed on longline vessels [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pelagic longline fishermen who did not take the buyout would lose access to major fishing grounds; the crews who sold out would exit fishing permanently and their boats could never be used to fish commercially anywhere in the world. Taxpayers would cover $30 million in appropriations plus the cost of a $20 million loan, and swordfish dealers would pay a fee of up to five cents per pound, while boaters over 18 feet fishing for tuna and billfish in the closed areas would need a $25 permit or live in one of seven Gulf states that would have to pay its share of the loan.

drawbacks.text: Fishermen who took the buyout would surrender every commercial fishing permit they held and their vessels would be banned from commercial fishing anywhere in the world forever, with criminal penalties of up to five years and forfeiture of the boat for violations — a permanent exit, not a temporary sacrifice [S3].

The bill authorizes $30 million in appropriations and a $20 million federal direct loan, with the loan repaid by fees on swordfish dealers and by $25 recreational permits or mandatory payments from seven Gulf states, so part of the cost lands on fish buyers and coastal boaters rather than only on the longline fleet [S3].

Closing areas can push fishing effort into the waters that remain open; the bill itself requires the government to monitor the Mid-Atlantic Bight for a net increase in longline vessels and to report back if the displacement worsens harm to marlin, sharks, and turtles [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The conservation case is strong on the bill's own record: several stocks were at a small fraction of healthy levels and longlines were a major source of the mortality. The buyout design is a fair attempt to spare the affected crews. The costs are real but bounded — a one-time appropriation and loan, a modest dealer fee, and a permanent exit for the fishermen who choose to sell. The main design risk is displaced fishing effort, which the bill monitors but does not fully solve.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee referred the bill to its fisheries subcommittee in June 2000, and it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Saxton of New Jersey introduced the bill on June 8, 2000, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Resources [S5].
On June 23, 2000, it was sent to the subcommittee on Fisheries Conservation, Wildlife and Oceans, with executive comment requested from the Commerce Department; that is the last action recorded [S5].
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill died in subcommittee without a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pelagic longline fishing businesses kept operating in the waters the bill would have closed, with no buyout, no fee, and no closures; the overfished swordfish and marlin stocks got nothing from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Jim Saxton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to the Natural Resources Committee.

for.name: Recreational billfish and tuna fishing community
for.role: Anglers and charter sector affected by longline bycatch
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed time-area closures of longline fishing during the 2000 debate over Atlantic highly migratory species; the bill's own findings cite the conflicts between longline and recreational fisheries.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the full committee and its fisheries subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Fisheries Conservation, Wildlife and Oceans subcommittee on June 23, 2000 and never brought it to a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Pelagic longline fishing industry
against.role: Commercial longline vessel owners facing closures and a permanent buyout
against.what_they_did: Worked against legislated time-area closures during the 2000 fishery-management fight, favoring management left to regulators rather than the fixed closures this bill wrote into law.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors and drew no recorded votes, so its support was bipartisan but thin; it died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would close large Atlantic and Gulf grounds to longlining and buy out many of the boats — up to $450,000 per permit holder — but those who sold out could never fish commercially again, and holdouts would lose the grounds. The industry's fishing method was the target because it kills large numbers of overfished marlin, sharks, and young swordfish as bycatch.

industries.industry: Recreational billfish and tuna fishing, including charter boats
industries.note: Fewer longlines in the closed zones would mean more marlin and swordfish to catch and less conflict with commercial gear; the trade-off is a $25 federal permit for boats over 18 feet fishing the closed areas, or state-level payments covering the recreational share of the loan.
The bill would hand the bought-out longline fleet's share of the swordfish catch quota to the hand-gear fleet, which lands fish with far less bycatch.

Dealers would deduct and forward a fee of up to five cents per pound on every pound of Atlantic swordfish sold to repay the $20 million federal loan, a modest pass-through cost that would reach swordfish buyers.
